exercises.prompt: Two friends, Alex and Sam, each play five games of chess over a tournament weekend. Alex wins three of his five games, and Sam also wins three of his five games — yet neither Alex nor Sam ever loses a game to the other. How is this possible? Work out an explanation, then reveal and compare.
exercises.answer: Alex and Sam never played each other at all — each played all five of their games against other opponents in the tournament, so their win counts have nothing to do with one another.
exercises.explanation: The riddle only feels paradoxical if you assume 'each plays five games' means they played each other; nothing in the setup actually says that.

exercises.prompt: What common English word, written in capital letters, still spells the same word when the page is turned upside-down (rotated 180 degrees)?
exercises.explanation: Rotate each letter of SWIMS 180 degrees and read in the new order: S stays S, W becomes M, I stays I, M becomes W, S stays S — spelling SWIMS again. NOON works the same way.

exercises.prompt: Buses on a route are scheduled to arrive every 10 minutes on average, but in practice they bunch up, so the actual gaps between buses vary — some only 2 minutes, others 18 minutes. If you show up at a uniformly random moment, is your expected wait for the next bus exactly 5 minutes, more than 5 minutes, or less than 5 minutes?
choices: It depends only on the bus color
exercises.explanation: This is the 'inspection paradox': a random arrival is more likely to land inside a longer gap simply because longer gaps take up more of the timeline, so the average gap you actually experience is longer than the schedule's average gap.

exercises.prompt: Which of these fruits is botanically a true berry: the banana or the strawberry?
exercises.explanation: Botanically, a berry develops from a single flower ovary and has flesh surrounding its seeds — bananas qualify, but strawberries don't: a strawberry is an 'aggregate accessory fruit' whose seeds each come from separate ovaries on the outside of the flesh.

exercises.prompt: Clock A is broken and permanently stopped, frozen at one fixed time. Clock B works, but runs consistently 1 minute slow every hour. Over the course of a year, counting only the exact instants when a clock's displayed time matches the real time, which clock is correct more often? Work it out, then reveal and compare.
exercises.answer: Clock A, the stopped one — by a wide margin. A 12-hour analog dial displays the same fixed time as the real time twice every 24 hours, about 730 times a year. Clock B loses 1 minute per hour, so it takes 720 hours (30 days) to drift through a full 12-hour cycle and land back on the correct time — only about 12 times a year.
exercises.explanation: This formalizes the old saying that a stopped clock is right twice a day — a clock that's merely inaccurate can, perhaps surprisingly, be correct far less often than one that isn't running at all.

exercises.prompt: Which is farther east: the easternmost tip of Brazil, or New York City?
choices: They sit at about the same longitude
It depends on the time of year
exercises.explanation: New York City sits around 74 degrees west longitude, while Brazil's easternmost point, near Joao Pessoa, is only about 35 degrees west — South America bulges much farther east than most mental maps suggest, putting large parts of Brazil east of the whole U.S. East Coast.

exercises.prompt: A resting human heart beats roughly 70 times a minute. Over an average 80-year lifetime, roughly how many total times does it beat?
exercises.explanation: 70 beats/min x 60 x 24 x 365 x 80 comes out to roughly 2.9 billion beats — close to 3 billion.

exercises.prompt: A man walks into a dark room holding just one match. Inside are a candle, an oil lamp, and a wood-burning stove, all unlit. Which does he light first?
exercises.explanation: Nothing else can be lit until the match itself is burning — an obvious first step the question tricks you into overlooking.

exercises.prompt: You flip a fair coin 4 times. Which specific outcome is more likely: the exact sequence HHHH, or the exact sequence HTHT?
choices: It depends on how the coin is flipped
exercises.explanation: Every specific sequence of 4 independent coin flips has the same probability, $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$. HTHT only feels more 'random' than HHHH because it looks less patterned — that intuition tracks how typical a sequence looks, not its actual probability.

exercises.prompt: What starts with T, ends with T, and is full of T?
exercises.explanation: "Teapot" starts and ends with T, and a teapot is typically full of tea.
